entries.ff95a509189b651933069a13e05077d9933f4983: <div sID="gen19893" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="11" osisID="Hos.11" sID="Hos.11"/> <div eID="gen19893" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19894" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen19895" type="x-p"/> In this chapter we have, I. The great goodness of God towards his people Israel, and the great things he had done for them, <reference osisRef="Hos.11.1">ver. 1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Hos.11.3">3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Hos.11.4">4</reference>. II. Their ungrateful conduct towards him, notwithstanding his favours towards them, <reference osisRef="Hos.11.2-Hos.11.4">ver. 2-4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Hos.11.7">7</reference>, <reference osisRef="Hos.11.12">12</reference>. III. Threatenings of wrath against them for their ingratitude and treachery, <reference osisRef="Hos.11.5-Hos.11.6">ver. 5, 6</reference>. IV. Mercy remembered in the midst of wrath, <reference osisRef="Hos.11.8-Hos.11.9">ver. 8, 9</reference>. V. Promises of what God would yet do for them, <reference osisRef="Hos.11.10-Hos.11.11">ver. 10, 11</reference>. VI. An honourable character given of Judah, <reference osisRef="Hos.11.12">ver. 12</reference>.
entries.ab84cfa140029e952bc81431cb7ad0119819ab98: <div eID="gen19895" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen19894" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">God's Goodness to Israel; The Ingratitude of Israel; God's Displeasure with Israel. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi>  730.)</title> <div sID="gen19896" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> When Israel <hi type="italic">was</hi> a child, then I loved him, and called my son out of Egypt. <hi type="super">2</hi> <hi type="italic">As</hi> they called them, so they went from them: they sacrificed unto Baalim, and burned incense to graven images. <hi type="super">3</hi> I taught Ephraim also to go, taking them by their arms; but they knew not that I healed them. <hi type="super">4</hi> I drew them with cords of a man, with bands of love: and I was to them as they that take off the yoke on their jaws, and I laid meat unto them. <hi type="super">5</hi> He shall not return into the land of Egypt, but the Assyrian shall be his king, because they refused to return. <hi type="super">6</hi> And the sword shall abide on his cities, and shall consume his branches, and devour <hi type="italic">them,</hi> because of their own counsels. <hi type="super">7</hi> And my people are bent to backsliding from me: though they called them to the most High, none at all would exalt <hi type="italic">him.</hi> <div eID="gen19896" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19897" type="x-p"/> Here we find, <div eID="gen19897" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19898" type="x-p"/> I. God very gracious to Israel. They were a people for whom he had done more than for any people under heaven, and to whom he had given more, which they are here, I will not say upbraided with (for God gives, and upbraids not), but put in mind of, as an aggravation of their sin and an encouragement to repentance. 1. He had a kindness for them when they were young (<reference osisRef="Hos.11.1">v. 1</reference>): <hi type="italic">When Israel was a child then I loved him;</hi> when they first began to multiply into a nation in Egypt God then <hi type="italic">set his love upon them,</hi> and <hi type="italic">chose them because he loved them,</hi> because he would love them, <reference osisRef="Deut.7.7-Deut.7.8">Deut. vii. 7, 8</reference>. When they were weak and helpless as children, foolish and froward as children, when they were outcasts, and children exposed, then God <hi type="italic">loved them;</hi> he pitied them, and testified his goodwill to them; he bore them as the nurse does the sucking child, nourished them, and suffered their manners. Note, Those that have grown up, nay, those that have grown old, ought often to reflect upon the goodness of God to them in their childhood. 2. He delivered them out of the house of bondage: <hi type="italic">I called my son out of Egypt,</hi> because a son, because a beloved son. When God demanded Israel's discharge from Pharaoh he called them <hi type="italic">his son,</hi> his <hi type="italic">first-born.</hi> Note, Those whom God loves he calls out of the bondage of sin and Satan into the glorious liberty of his children. These words are said to have been fulfilled in Christ, when, upon the death of Herod, he and his parents were <hi type="italic">called out of Egypt</hi> (<reference osisRef="Matt.2.15">Matt. ii. 15</reference>), so that the words have a double aspect, speaking historically of the calling of Israel out of Egypt and prophetically of the bringing of Christ thence; and the former was a type of the latter, and a pledge and earnest of the many and great favours God had in reserve for that people, especially the sending of his Son into the world, and the bringing him again into the land of Israel when they had unkindly driven him out, and he might justly never have returned. The calling of Christ out of Egypt was a figure of the calling of all that are his, through him, out of spiritual slavery. 3. He gave them a good education, took care of them, took pains with them, not only as a father or tutor, but, such is the condescension of divine grace, as a mother or nurse (<reference osisRef="Hos.11.3">v. 3</reference>): <hi type="italic">I taught Ephraim also to go,</hi> as a child in leading-strings is taught. When they were in the wilderness God led them by the pillar of cloud and fire, showed them the way in which they should go, and bore them up, <hi type="italic">taking them by the arms. He taught them to go</hi> in the way of his commandments, by the institutions of the ceremonial law, which were as tutors and governors to that people under age. He took them by the arms, to guide them, that they might not stray, and to hold them up, that they might not stumble and fall. God's spiritual Israel are thus supported. <hi type="italic">Thou has holden me by my right hand,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.73.23">Ps. lxxiii. 23</reference>. 4. When any thing was amiss with them, or they were ever so little out of order, he was their physician: "<hi type="italic">I healed them;</hi> I not only took a tender care of them (a friend may do that), but wrought an effectual cure: it is a God only that can do that. <hi type="italic">I am the Lord that healeth thee</hi> (<reference osisRef="Exod.15.26">Exod. xv. 26</reference>), that redresseth all thy grievances." 5. He brought them into his service by mild and gentle methods (<reference osisRef="Hos.11.4">v. 4</reference>): <hi type="italic">I drew them with cords of a man, with bands of love.</hi> Note, It is God's work to draw poor souls to himself; and none can come to him except he draw them, <reference osisRef="John.6.44">John vi. 44</reference>. He draws, (1.) <hi type="italic">With the cords of a man,</hi> with such cords as men draw with that have a principle of humanity, or such cords as men are drawn with; he dealt with them <hi type="italic">as men,</hi> in an equitable rational way, in an easy gentle way, <hi type="italic">with the cords of Adam.</hi> He dealt with them as with Adam in innocency, bringing them at once into a paradise, and into covenant with himself. (2.) <hi type="italic">With bands of love,</hi> or <hi type="italic">cartropes</hi> of love. This word signifies stronger cords than the former. He did not drive them by force into his service, whether they would or no, nor rule them with rigour, nor detain them by violence, but his attractives were all loving and endearing, all sweet and gentle, that he might overcome them with kindness. Moses, whom he made their guide, was the meekest man in the world. <hi type="italic">Kindnesses</hi> among men we commonly call <hi type="italic">obligations,</hi> or <hi type="italic">bonds,</hi> bonds of love. Thus God <hi type="italic">draws with the savour of his good ointments</hi> (<reference osisRef="Song.1.4">Cant. i. 4</reference>), draws <hi type="italic">with lovingkindness,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.31.3">Jer. xxxi. 3</reference>. Thus God deals with us, and we must deal in like manner with those that are under our instruction and government, deal rationally and mildly with them. 6. He eased them of the burdens they had been long groaning under: <hi type="italic">I was to them as those that take off the yoke on their jaws,</hi> alluding to the care of the good husbandman, who is merciful to his beast, and will not tire him with hard and constant labour. Probably, in those times, the yoke on the neck of the oxen was fastened with some bridle, or headstall, over the jaws, which <hi type="italic">muzzled the mouth of the ox.</hi> Israel in Egypt were thus restrained from the enjoyments of their comforts and constrained to hard labour; but God eased them, <hi type="italic">removed their shoulder from the burden,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.81.6">Ps. lxxxi. 6</reference>. Note, Liberty is a great mercy, especially out of bondage. 7. He supplied them with food convenient. In Egypt they fared hard, but, when God brought them out, he <hi type="italic">laid meat unto them,</hi> as the husbandman, when he has unyoked his cattle, fodders them. God rained manna about their camp, bread from heaven, angels' food; other creatures <hi type="italic">seek their meat,</hi> but God laid meat to his own people, as we do to our children, was himself their caterer and carver, anticipated <hi type="italic">them with the blessings of goodness.</hi> <div eID="gen19898" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19899" type="x-p"/> II. Here is Israel very ungrateful to God. <div eID="gen19899" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19900" type="x-p"/> 1. They were deaf and disobedient to his voice. He spoke to them by his messengers, Moses and his other prophets, called them from their sins, called them to himself, to their work and duty; but <hi type="italic">as they called them so they went from them;</hi> they rebelled in those particular instances wherein they were admonished; the more pressing and importunate the prophets were with them, to persuade them to that which was good, the more refractory they were, and the more resolute in their evil ways, disobeying for disobedience-sake. This foolishness is bound in the hearts of children, who, as soon as they are taught to go, will go from those that call them. <div eID="gen19900" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19901" type="x-p"/> 2. They were fond of idols, and worshipped them: They <hi type="italic">sacrificed to Baalim,</hi> first one Baal and then another, and <hi type="italic">burnt incense to graven images,</hi> though they were called to by the prophets of the Lord again and again not to do this abominable thing which he hated. Idolatry was the sin which from the beginning, and all along, had most easily beset them. <div eID="gen19901" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19902" type="x-p"/> 3. They were regardless of God, and of his favours to them: <hi type="italic">They knew not that I healed them.</hi> They looked only at Moses and Aaron, the instruments of their relief, and, when any thing was amiss, quarrelled with them, but looked not through them to God who employed them. Or, When God corrected them, and kept them under a severe discipline, they understood not that it was for their good, and that God thereby <hi type="italic">healed them,</hi> and it was necessary for the perfecting of their cure, else they would have been better reconciled to the methods God took. Note, Ignorance is at the bottom of ingratitude, <reference osisRef="Hos.2.8">ch. ii. 8</reference>. <div eID="gen19902" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19903" type="x-p"/> 4. They were strongly inclined to apostasy. This is the blackest article in the charge (<reference osisRef="Hos.11.7">v. 7</reference>): <hi type="italic">My people are bent to backsliding from me.</hi> Every word here is aggravating. (1.) They <hi type="italic">backslide.</hi> There is no hold of them, no stedfastness in them; they seem to come forward, towards God, but they quickly slide back again, and are as a deceitful bow. (2.) They backslide <hi type="italic">from me,</hi> from God, the chief good, the fountain of life and living waters, from their God who never turned from them, nor war as a wilderness to them. (3.) They are <hi type="italic">bent to backslide;</hi> they are ready to sin; there is in their natures a propensity to that which is evil; at the best they hang in suspense between God and the world, so that a little thing serves to draw them the wrong way; they are forward to close with every temptation. It also intimates that they are resolute in sin; their hearts are <hi type="italic">fully set in them to do evil</hi> the bias is strong that way; and they persist in their backslidings, whatever is said or done to stop them; and yet, (4.) "They are, in profession, <hi type="italic">my people.</hi> They are <hi type="italic">called by my name,</hi> and profess relation to me; they are mine, whom I have done much for and expect much from, whom I have <hi type="italic">nourished</hi> and <hi type="italic">brought up, as children,</hi> and yet they backslide <hi type="italic">from me.</hi>" Note, In our repentance we ought to lament not only our backslidings, but our <hi type="italic">bent to backslide,</hi> not only our actual transgressions, but our original corruption, the sin that dwells in us, the carnal mind. <div eID="gen19903" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19904" type="x-p"/> 5. They were strangely averse to repentance and reformation. Here are two expressions of their obstinacy:— (1.) <hi type="italic">They refused to return,</hi> <reference osisRef="Hos.11.5">v. 5</reference>. So much were they bent to backslide that, though they could not but find, upon trial, the folly of their backslidings, and that when they forsook God they changed for the worse, yet they went on frowardly. <hi type="italic">I have loved strangers, and after them I will go.</hi> They were commanded to return, were courted and entreated to return, were promised that if they would they should be kindly received, but they refused. (2.) Though <hi type="italic">they called them to the Most High.</hi> God's prophets and ministers called them to return to the God from whom they had revolted, to the most high God, from whom they had sunk into this wretched degeneracy; they called them from the worship of the idols, which were so much below them, and the worship of which was therefore their disparagement, to the true God, who was so much above them, and the worship of whom was therefore their preferment; they called them from this earth to high and heavenly things; but they called in vain. <hi type="italic">None at all would exalt him.</hi> Though he is the most high God they would not acknowledge him to be so, would do nothing to honour him nor give him the glory due to his name. Or, They would not <hi type="italic">exalt themselves,</hi> would not rise out of that state of apostasy and misery into which they had precipitated themselves; but there they contentedly lay still, would not lift up their heads nor lift up their souls. Note, God's faithful ministers have taken a great deal of pains, to no purpose, with backsliding children, have called them to the Most High; but none would stir, <hi type="italic">none at all would exalt him.</hi> <div eID="gen19904" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19905" type="x-p"/> III. Here is God very angry, and justly so, with Israel; see what are the tokens of God's displeasure with which they are here threatened. 1. God, who brought them out of Egypt, to take them for a people to himself, since they would not be faithful to him, shall bring them into a worse condition than he at first found them in (<reference osisRef="Hos.11.5">v. 5</reference>): "<hi type="italic">He shall not return into the land of Egypt,</hi> though that was a house of bondage grievous enough; but he shall go into a harder service, for <hi type="italic">the Assyrian shall be his king,</hi> who will use him worse than ever Pharaoh did." They shall not return into Egypt, which lies near, where they may hear often from their own country, and whence they may hope shortly to return to it again; but they shall be carried into Assyria, which lies much more remote, and where they shall be cut off from all correspondence with their own land and from all hopes of returning to it, and justly, because <hi type="italic">they refused to return.</hi> Note, Those that will not return to the duties they have left cannot expect to return to the comforts they have lost. 2. God, who gave them Canaan, that good land, and a very safe and comfortable settlement in it, shall bring his judgments upon them there, which shall make their habitation unsafe and uncomfortable (<reference osisRef="Hos.11.6">v. 6</reference>): <hi type="italic">The sword</hi> shall come upon them, the sword of war, the sword of a foreign enemy, prevailing against them and triumphing over them. (1.) This judgment shall spread far. The sword shall fasten upon their <hi type="italic">cities,</hi> those nests of people and store-houses of wealth; it shall likewise reach to their <hi type="italic">branches,</hi> the country villages (so some), the citizens themselves (so others), or the <hi type="italic">bars</hi> (so the word signifies) and gates of their city, or all the branches of their revenue and wealth, or their children, the branches of their families. (2.) It shall last long: It shall <hi type="italic">abide on their cities.</hi> David thought <hi type="italic">three months</hi> flying before his enemies was the only judgment of the three that was to be excepted against; but this <hi type="italic">sword</hi> shall abide much longer than three months on the cities of Israel. They continued their rebellions against God, and therefore God continued his judgments on them. (3.) It shall <hi type="italic">make a full end:</hi> It shall <hi type="italic">consume their branches, and devour them,</hi> and lay all waste, and this <hi type="italic">because of their own counsels,</hi> that is, because they would have their own projects, which God therefore, in a way of righteous judgment, gave them up to. Note, The confusion of sinners is owing to their contrivance. God's counsels would have saved them, but their own counsels ruined them.
entries.e55ea156d2275e2c313360a082e4e9b02d996b44: <div eID="gen19905" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Divine Forbearance. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 730.)</title> <div sID="gen19906" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">8</hi> How shall I give thee up, Ephraim? <hi type="italic">how</hi> shall I deliver thee, Israel? how shall I make thee as Admah? <hi type="italic">how</hi> shall I set thee as Zeboim? mine heart is turned within me, my repentings are kindled together. <hi type="super">9</hi> I will not execute the fierceness of mine anger, I will not return to destroy Ephraim: for I <hi type="italic">am</hi> God, and not man; the Holy One in the midst of thee: and I will not enter into the city. <hi type="super">10</hi> They shall walk after the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> : he shall roar like a lion: when he shall roar, then the children shall tremble from the west. <hi type="super">11</hi> They shall tremble as a bird out of Egypt, and as a dove out of the land of Assyria: and I will place them in their houses, saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <hi type="super">12</hi> Ephraim compasseth me about with lies, and the house of Israel with deceit: but Judah yet ruleth with God, and is faithful with the saints. <div eID="gen19906" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19907" type="x-p"/> In these verses we have, <div eID="gen19907" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19908" type="x-p"/> I. God's wonderful backwardness to destroy Israel (<reference osisRef="Hos.11.8-Hos.11.9">v. 8, 9</reference>): <hi type="italic">How shall I give thee up?</hi> Here observe, <div eID="gen19908" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19909" type="x-p"/> 1. God's gracious debate within himself concerning Israel's case, a debate between justice and mercy, in which victory plainly inclines to mercy's side. Be astonished, O heavens! at this, and wonder, O earth! at the glory of God's goodness. Not that there are any such struggles in God as there are in us, or that he is ever fluctuating or unresolved; no, he is in one mind, and knows it; but they are expressions after the manner of men, designed to show what severity the sin of Israel had deserved, and yet how divine grace would be glorified in sparing them notwithstanding. The connexion of this with what goes before is very surprising; it was said of Israel (<reference osisRef="Hos.11.7">v. 7</reference>) that they were <hi type="italic">bent to backslide from God,</hi> that though they were called to him they <hi type="italic">would not exalt him,</hi> upon which, one would think, it should have followed, "Now I am determined to destroy them, and never show them mercy any more." No, such is the sovereignty of mercy, such the freeness, the fulness, of divine grace, that it follows immediately, <hi type="italic">How shall I give thee up?</hi> See here, (1.) The proposals that justice makes concerning Israel, the suggestion of which is here implied. Let Ephraim be given up, as an incorrigible son is given up to be disinherited, as an incurable patient is given over by his physician. Let him be given up to ruin. Let Israel be delivered into the enemy's hand, as a lamb to the lion to be torn in pieces; let them be made as Admah and set as Zeboim, the two cities that with Sodom and Gomorrah were destroyed by fire and brimstone rained from heaven upon them; let them be utterly and irreparably ruined, and be made as like these cities in desolation as they have been in sin. Let that curse which is written in the law be executed upon them, that the <hi type="italic">whole land</hi> shall be <hi type="italic">brimstone and salt, like the overthrow of Sodom and Gomorrah, Admah and Zeboim,</hi> <reference osisRef="Deut.29.23">Deut. xxix. 23</reference>. Ephraim and Israel deserve to be thus abandoned, and God will do them no wrong if he deal thus with them. (2.) The opposition that mercy makes to these proposals: <hi type="italic">How shall I do it?</hi> As the tender father reasons with himself, "How can I cast off my untoward son? for he is my son, though he be untoward; how can I find in my heart to do it?" Thus, "Ephraim has been a dear son, a pleasant child: <hi type="italic">How can I do it?</hi> He is ripe for ruin; judgments stand ready to seize him; there wants nothing but <hi type="italic">giving him up,</hi> but I cannot do it. They have been a people near unto me; there are yet some good among them; theirs are the children of the covenant; if they be ruined, the enemy will triumph; it may be they will yet repent and reform; and therefore how can I do it?" Note, The God of heaven is slow to anger, and is especially loth to abandon a people to utter ruin that have been in special relation to him. See how mercy works upon the mention of those severe proceedings: <hi type="italic">My heart is turned within me,</hi> as we say, Our heart fails us, when we come to do a thing that is against the grain with us. God speaks as if he were conscious to himself of a strange striving of affections in compassion to Israel: as <reference osisRef="Lam.1.20">Lam. i. 20</reference>, <hi type="italic">My bowels are troubled; my heart is turned within me.</hi> As it follows here, <hi type="italic">My repentings are kindled together.</hi> His bowels yearned towards them, and <hi type="italic">his soul was grieved</hi> for their sin and <hi type="italic">misery,</hi> <reference osisRef="Judg.10.16">Judg. x. 16</reference>. Compare <reference osisRef="Jer.31.20">Jer. xxxi. 20</reference>. <hi type="italic">Since I spoke against him my bowels are troubled for him.</hi> When God was to give up his Son to be a sacrifice for sin, and a Saviour for sinners, he did not say, How shall I give him up? No, he <hi type="italic">spared not his own Son;</hi> it <hi type="italic">pleased the Lord to bruise him;</hi> and <hi type="italic">therefore</hi> God spared not him, that he might spare us. But this is only the language of the day of his patience; when men have sinned that away, and the great day of his wrath comes, then no difficulty is made of it; nay, <hi type="italic">I will laugh at their calamity.</hi> <div eID="gen19909" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19910" type="x-p"/> 2. His gracious determination of this debate. After a long contest mercy in the issue rejoices against judgment, has the last word, and carries the day, <reference osisRef="Hos.11.9">v. 9</reference>. It is decreed that the reprieve shall be lengthened out yet longer, and <hi type="italic">I will not</hi> now <hi type="italic">execute the fierceness of my anger,</hi> though I am angry; though they shall not go altogether unpunished, yet he will mitigate the sentence and abate the rigour of it. He will show himself to be justly angry, but not implacably so; they shall be corrected, but not consumed. <hi type="italic">I will not return to destroy Ephraim;</hi> the judgments that have been inflicted shall not be repeated, shall not go so deep as they have deserved. He will not <hi type="italic">return to destroy,</hi> as soldiers, when they have pillaged a town once, return a second time, to take more, as when <hi type="italic">what the palmer-worm has left the locust has eaten.</hi> It is added, in the close of the <reference osisRef="Hos.11.9">verse</reference>, "<hi type="italic">I will not enter into the city,</hi> into Samaria, or any other of their cities; I will not enter into them as an enemy, utterly to destroy them, and lay them waste, as I did the cities of Admah and Zeboim." <div eID="gen19910" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19911" type="x-p"/> 3. The ground and reason of this determination: <hi type="italic">For I am God and not man, the Holy One of Israel.</hi> To encourage them, to hope that they shall find mercy, consider, (1.) What he is in himself: <hi type="italic">He is God, and not man,</hi> as in other things, so in pardoning sin and sparing sinners. If they had offended a man like themselves, he would not, he could not have borne it; his passion would have overpowered his compassion, and he would have executed the fierceness of his anger; but <hi type="italic">I am God, and not man.</hi> He is <hi type="italic">Lord of his anger,</hi> whereas men's anger commonly lords it over them. If an earthly prince were in such a strait between justice and mercy, he would be at a loss how to compromise the matter between them; but he who is God, and not man, knows how to find out an expedient to secure the honour of his justice and yet advance the honour of his mercy. Man's compassions are nothing in comparison with the tender mercies of our God, whose thoughts and ways, in receiving returning sinners, are as much above ours as heaven is above the earth, <reference osisRef="Isa.55.9">Isa. lv. 9</reference>. Note, It is a great encouragement to our hope in God's mercies to remember that he is <hi type="italic">God, and not man.</hi> He is <hi type="italic">the Holy One.</hi> One would think this were a reason why he should reject such a provoking people. No; God knows how to spare and pardon poor sinners, not only without any reproach to his holiness, but very much to the honour of it, as he is <hi type="italic">faithful and just to forgive us our sins,</hi> and therein <hi type="italic">declares his righteousness,</hi> now Christ has purchased the pardon and he has promised it. (2.) What he is to them; he is the <hi type="italic">Holy One in the midst of thee;</hi> his holiness is engaged for the good of his church, and even in this corrupt and degenerate land and age there were some that gave thanks at the remembrance of his holiness, and he required of them all to be <hi type="italic">holy as he is,</hi> <reference osisRef="Lev.19.2">Lev. xix. 2</reference>. As long as we have the <hi type="italic">Holy One in the midst of us</hi> we are safe and well; but woe to us when he leaves us! Note, Those who submit to the influence may take the comfort of God's holiness. <div eID="gen19911" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19912" type="x-p"/> II. Here is his wonderful forwardness to do good for Israel, which appears in this, that he will qualify them to receive the good he designs for them (<reference osisRef="Hos.11.10-Hos.11.11">v. 10, 11</reference>): <hi type="italic">They shall walk after the Lord.</hi> This respects the same favour with that (<reference osisRef="Hos.3.5">ch. iii. 5</reference>), <hi type="italic">They shall return, and seek the Lord their God;</hi> it is spoken of the ten tribes, and had its accomplishment, in part, in the return of some of them with those of the two tribes in Ezra's time; but it had its more full accomplishment in God's spiritual Israel, the gospel-church, brought together and incorporated by the gospel of Christ. The ancient Jews referred it to the time of the Messiah; the learned Dr. Pocock looks upon it as a prophecy of Christ's coming to preach the gospel to the dispersed children of Israel, the children of God that were scattered abroad. And then observe, 1. How they were to be called and brought together: <hi type="italic">The Lord shall roar like a lion.</hi> The <hi type="italic">word of the Lord</hi> (so says the Chaldee) <hi type="italic">shall be as a lion that roars.</hi> Christ is called <hi type="italic">the lion of the tribe of Judah,</hi> and his gospel, in the beginning of it, was <hi type="italic">the voice of one crying in the wilderness.</hi> When Christ cried with a loud voice it was as <hi type="italic">when a lion roared,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rev.10.3">Rev. x. 3</reference>. The voice of the gospel was heard afar, as the <hi type="italic">roaring of a lion,</hi> and it was a <hi type="italic">mighty voice.</hi> See <reference osisRef="Joel.3.16">Joel iii. 16</reference>. 2. What impression this call should make upon them, such an impression as the roaring of a lion makes upon all the beasts of the forest: <hi type="italic">When he shall roar then the children shall tremble.</hi> See <reference osisRef="Amos.3.8">Amos iii. 8</reference>, <hi type="italic">The lion has roared; the Lord</hi> God <hi type="italic">has spoken;</hi> and then <hi type="italic">who will not fear?</hi> When those whose hearts the gospel reached trembled, and were astonished, and cried out, <hi type="italic">What shall we do?</hi>—when they were by it put upon working out their salvation, and worshipping God with fear and trembling, then this promise was fulfilled. <hi type="italic">The children shall tremble from the west.</hi> The dispersed Jews were carried eastward, to Assyria and Babylon, and those that returned came from the east; therefore this seems to have reference to the calling of the Gentiles that lay westward from Canaan, for that way especially the gospel spread. They shall <hi type="italic">tremble;</hi> they shall move and come with trembling, with care and haste, <hi type="italic">from the west,</hi> from the nations that lay that way, to the mountain of the Lord (<reference osisRef="Isa.2.3">Isa. ii. 3</reference>), to the gospel-Jerusalem, upon hearing the alarm of the gospel. The apostle speaks of <hi type="italic">mighty signs and wonders</hi> that were wrought by the preaching of the gospel from <hi type="italic">Jerusalem round about to Illyricum,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rom.15.19">Rom. xv. 19</reference>. Then the children trembled from the west. And, whereas Israel after the flesh was dispersed in Egypt and Assyria, it is promised that they shall be effectually summoned thence (<reference osisRef="Hos.11.11">v. 11</reference>): <hi type="italic">They shall tremble;</hi> they shall come trembling, and with all haste, <hi type="italic">as a bird</hi> upon the wing, <hi type="italic">out of Egypt,</hi> and <hi type="italic">as a dove out of the land of Assyria;</hi> a dove is noted for swift and constant flight, especially when she flies <hi type="italic">to her windows,</hi> which the flocking of Jews and Gentiles to the church is here compared to, as it is <reference osisRef="Isa.60.8">Isa. lx. 8</reference>. Wherever those are that belong to the election of grace—east, west, north, or south—they shall <hi type="italic">hear the joyful sound,</hi> and be wrought upon by it; those of Egypt and Assyria shall come together; those that lay most remote from each other shall meet in Christ, and be incorporated in the church. Of the uniting of Egypt and Assyria, it was prophesied, <reference osisRef="Isa.19.23">Isa. xix. 23</reference>. 3. What effect these impressions should have upon them. Being <hi type="italic">moved with fear,</hi> they shall flee to the ark: <hi type="italic">They shall walk after the Lord,</hi> after <hi type="italic">the service of the Lord</hi> (so the Chaldee); they shall take the Lord Christ for their <hi type="italic">leader and commander;</hi> they shall enlist themselves under him as the captain of their salvation, and give up themselves to the direction of the Spirit as their guide by the word; they shall <hi type="italic">leave all</hi> to <hi type="italic">follow Christ,</hi> as becomes <hi type="italic">disciples.</hi> Note, Our holy trembling at the word of Christ will draw us to him, not drive us from him. When he <hi type="italic">roars like a lion</hi> the slaves tremble and flee from him, the children tremble and flee to him. 4. What entertainment they shall meet with at their return (<reference osisRef="Hos.11.11">v. 11</reference>): <hi type="italic">I will place them in their houses</hi> (all those that come at the gospel-call shall have a place and a name in the gospel-church, in the particular churches which are their houses, to which they pertain; they shall dwell in God, and be at home in him, both easy and safe, as a man in his own house; they shall have mansions, for there are many in <hi type="italic">our Father's house</hi>), in his tabernacle on earth and his temple in heaven, in <hi type="italic">everlasting habitations,</hi> which may be called <hi type="italic">their houses,</hi> for they are <hi type="italic">the lot</hi> they shall stand in <hi type="italic">at the end of the days.</hi> <div eID="gen19912" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19913" type="x-p"/> III. Here is a sad complaint of the treachery of Ephraim and Israel, which may be an intimation that it is not Israel after the flesh, but the spiritual Israel, to whom the foregoing promises belong, for as for this Ephraim, this Israel, they <hi type="italic">compass God about with lies and deceit;</hi> all their services of him, when they pretended to compass his altar, were feigned and hypocritical; when they surrounded him with their prayers and praises, every one having a petition to present to him, they <hi type="italic">lied to him with their mouth and flattered him with their tongue;</hi> their pretensions were so fair, and yet their intentions so foul, that they would, if possible, have imposed upon God himself. Their professions and promises were all a cheat, and yet with these they thought to compass God about, to enclose him as it were, to keep him among them, and prevent his leaving them. <div eID="gen19913" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen19914" type="x-p"/> IV. Here is a pleasant commendation of the integrity of the two tribes, which they held fast, and this comes in as an aggravation of the perfidiousness of the ten tribes, and a reason why God had that mercy in store for Judah which he had not for Israel (<reference osisRef="Hos.1.6-Hos.1.7">ch. i. 6, 7</reference>), for <hi type="italic">Judah yet rules with God and is faithful with the saints,</hi> or <hi type="italic">with the Most Holy.</hi> 1. <hi type="italic">Judah rules with God,</hi> that is, he serves God, and the service of God is not only true liberty and freedom, but it is dignity and dominion. <hi type="italic">Judah rules,</hi> that is, the princes and governors of Judah <hi type="italic">rule with God;</hi> they use their power for him, for his honour, and the support of his interest. Those <hi type="italic">rule with God</hi> that <hi type="italic">rule in the fear of God</hi> (<reference osisRef="2Sam.23.3">2 Sam. xxiii. 3</reference>), and it is their honour to do so, and their praise shall be <hi type="italic">of God,</hi> as Judah's here is. Judah is <hi type="italic">Israel—a prince with God.</hi> 2. He is <hi type="italic">faithful with the holy God,</hi> keeps close to his worship and <hi type="italic">to his saints,</hi> with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, whose steps they faithfully tread in. They <hi type="italic">walk in the way of good men;</hi> and those that do so <hi type="italic">rule with God,</hi> they have a mighty interest in Heaven. Judah <hi type="italic">yet</hi> does thus, which intimates that the time would come when Judah also would revolt and degenerate. Note, When we see how many there are that compass God about <hi type="italic">with lies and deceit</hi> it may be a comfort to us to think that God has his remnant that cleave to him with purpose of heart, and are faithful to his saints; and for those who are thus faithful unto death is reserved a crown of life, when hypocrites and all liars shall have their portion without.  <chapter eID="Hos.11"/> <div eID="gen19914" type="x-p"/>

entries.cb36ca3352340a78c5a9e978c36412638abb32ff: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12384"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 11</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Hos.11.1-Hos.11.12">Ho 11:1-12</reference>. God's Former Benefits, and Israel's Ingratitude Resulting in Punishment, Yet Jehovah Promises Restoration at Last.</title> <div sID="gen22681" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="Hos.11.5">Ho 11:5</reference> shows this prophecy was uttered after the league made with Egypt (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.17.4">2Ki 17:4</reference>).<div eID="gen22681" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22682" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12384"/><hi type="bold">1. Israel ... called my son out of Egypt--</hi>Bengel translates, "From the time that he (Israel) was in Egypt, I called him My son," which the parallelism proves. So <reference osisRef="Hos.12.9">Ho 12:9</reference> and <reference osisRef="Hos.13.4">Ho 13:4</reference> use "from ... Egypt," for "from the time that thou didst sojourn in Egypt." <reference osisRef="Exod.4.22">Ex 4:22</reference> also shows that Israel was called by God, "My son," from the time of his Egyptian sojourn (<reference osisRef="Isa.43.1">Is 43:1</reference>). God is always said to have led or brought forth, not to have "called," Israel from Egypt. <reference osisRef="Matt.2.15">Mt 2:15</reference>, therefore, in quoting this prophecy (typically and primarily referring to Israel, antitypically and fully to Messiah), applies it to Jesus' sojourn in Egypt, not His return from it. Even from His infancy, partly spent in Egypt, God called Him His son. God included Messiah, and Israel for Messiah's sake, in one common love, and therefore in one common prophecy. Messiah's people and Himself are one, as the Head and the body. <reference osisRef="Isa.49.3">Is 49:3</reference> calls Him "Israel." The same general reason, danger of extinction, caused the infant Jesus, and Israel in its national infancy (compare <reference osisRef="Gen.42.1-Gen.43.34">Ge 42:1-43:34</reference>; 45:18; 46:3, 4; <reference osisRef="Ezek.16.4-Ezek.16.6">Eze 16:4-6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.31.20">Jr 31:20</reference>) to sojourn in Egypt. So He, and His spiritual Israel, are already called "God's sons" while yet in the Egypt of the world. <div eID="gen22682" type="x-p"/>
entries.4c9c6188fabccd27c9797feb1de11f4d167b9c56: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12385"/><div sID="gen22683" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12385"/><hi type="bold">2. As they called them--</hi>"they," namely, monitors sent by Me. "Called," in <reference osisRef="Hos.11.1">Ho 11:1</reference>, suggests the idea of the many subsequent calls by the prophets.<div eID="gen22683" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22684" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">went from them--</hi>turned away in contempt (<reference osisRef="Jer.2.27">Jr 2:27</reference>).<div eID="gen22684" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22685" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Baalim--</hi>images of Baal, set up in various places. <div eID="gen22685" type="x-p"/>
entries.9d8ec6e05d2942f1009b21dfa6082e9075ad4acf: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12386"/><div sID="gen22686" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12386"/><hi type="bold">3. taught ... to go--</hi>literally, "to use his feet." Compare a similar image, <reference osisRef="Deut.1.31">De 1:31</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.8.2">8:2</reference>, 5, 15; 32:10, 11; <reference osisRef="Neh.9.21">Ne 9:21</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.63.9">Is 63:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Amos.2.10">Am 2:10</reference>. God bore them as a parent does an infant, unable to supply itself, so that it has no anxiety about food, raiment, and its going forth. <reference osisRef="Acts.13.18">Ac 13:18</reference>, which probably refers to this passage of Hosea; He took them by the arms, to guide them that they might not stray, and to hold them up that they might not stumble.<div eID="gen22686" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22687" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">knew not that I healed them--</hi>that is, that My design was to restore them spiritually and temporally (<reference osisRef="Exod.15.26">Ex 15:26</reference>). <div eID="gen22687" type="x-p"/>
entries.4186ee8b8a007cc779108f8c98593df969778c4a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12387"/><div sID="gen22688" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12387"/><hi type="bold">4. cords of a man--</hi>parallel to "bands of love"; not such cords as oxen are led by, but humane methods, such as men employ when inducing others, as for instance, a father drawing his child, by leading-strings, teaching him to go (<reference osisRef="Hos.11.1">Ho 11:1</reference>).<div eID="gen22688" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22689" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">I was ... as they that take off the yoke on their jaws ... I laid meat--</hi>as the humane husbandman occasionally loosens the straps under the jaws by which the yoke is bound on the neck of oxen and lays food before them to eat. An appropriate image of God's deliverance of Israel from the Egyptian yoke, and of His feeding them in the wilderness. <div eID="gen22689" type="x-p"/>
entries.69847f4a625cf1bc1dcc039a72b24fd2b61c8d58: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12388"/><div sID="gen22690" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12388"/><hi type="bold">5. He shall not return into ... Egypt--</hi>namely, to seek help against Assyria (compare <reference osisRef="Hos.7.11">Ho 7:11</reference>), as Israel lately had done (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.17.4">2Ki 17:4</reference>), after having revolted from Assyria, to whom they had been tributary from the times of Menahem (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.15.19">2Ki 15:19</reference>). In a figurative sense, "he shall return to Egypt" (<reference osisRef="Hos.9.3">Ho 9:3</reference>), that is, to Egypt-like bondage; also many Jewish fugitives were literally to return to Egypt, when the Holy Land was to be in Assyrian and Chaldean hands.<div eID="gen22690" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22691" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Assyrian shall be his king--</hi>instead of having kings of their own, and Egypt as their auxiliary.<div eID="gen22691" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22692" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">because they refused to return--</hi>just retribution. They would not return (spiritually) to God, therefore they shall not return (corporally) to Egypt, the object of their desire. <div eID="gen22692" type="x-p"/>
entries.c7d22528e8792300b9348f6bb9db69250a59d38f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12389"/><div sID="gen22693" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12389"/><hi type="bold">6. abide--</hi>or, "fall upon" [Calvin].<div eID="gen22693" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22694" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">branches--</hi>that is, his villages, which are the branches or dependencies of the cities [Calvin]. Grotius translates, "his bars" (so <reference osisRef="Lam.2.9">La 2:9</reference>), that is, the warriors who were the bulwarks of the state. Compare <reference osisRef="Hos.4.18">Ho 4:18</reference>, "rulers" (Margin), "shields" (<reference osisRef="Ps.47.9">Psa 47:9</reference>).<div eID="gen22694" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22695" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">because of their own counsels--</hi>in worshipping idols, and relying on Egypt (compare <reference osisRef="Hos.10.6">Ho 10:6</reference>). <div eID="gen22695" type="x-p"/>
entries.ea7aedb3602cefc44e2deef652ddce489c79de26: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12390"/><div sID="gen22696" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12390"/><hi type="bold">7. bent to backsliding--</hi>Not only do they backslide, and that too from Me, their "chief good," but they are bent upon it. Though they (the prophets) called them (the Israelites) to the Most High (from their idols), "none would exalt (that is, extol or honor) Him." To exalt God, they must cease to be "bent on backsliding," and must lift themselves upwards. <div eID="gen22696" type="x-p"/>
entries.f780f7ee969a71f812c94773b15cb55df846f6ad: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12391"/><div sID="gen22697" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12391"/><hi type="bold">8. as Admah ... Zeboim--</hi>among the cities, including Sodom and Gomorrah, irretrievably overthrown (<reference osisRef="Deut.29.23">De 29:23</reference>).<div eID="gen22697" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22698" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">heart is turned within me--</hi>with the deepest compassion, so as not to execute My threat (<reference osisRef="Lam.1.20">La 1:20</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="Gen.43.30">Ge 43:30</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Kgs.3.26">1Ki 3:26</reference>). So the phrase is used of a new turn given to the feeling (<reference osisRef="Ps.105.25">Psa 105:25</reference>).<div eID="gen22698" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22699" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">repentings--</hi>God speaks according to human modes of thought (<reference osisRef="Num.23.19">Nu 23:19</reference>). God's seeming change is in accordance with His secret everlasting purpose of love to His people, to magnify His grace after their desperate rebellion. <div eID="gen22699" type="x-p"/>
entries.9dae4aca74d959915dcbef4db8009d40f89bfd04: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12392"/><div sID="gen22700" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12392"/><hi type="bold">9. I will not return to destroy Ephraim--</hi>that is, I will no more, as in past times, destroy Ephraim. The destruction primarily meant is probably that by Tiglath-pileser, who, as the Jewish king Ahaz' ally against Pekah of Israel and Rezin of Syria, deprived Israel of Gilead, Galilee, and Naphtali (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.15.29">2Ki 15:29</reference>). The ulterior reference is to the long dispersion hereafter, to be ended by God's covenant mercy restoring His people, not for their merits, but of His grace.<div eID="gen22700" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22701" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">God, ... not man--</hi>not dealing as man would, with implacable wrath under awful provocation (<reference osisRef="Isa.55.7-Isa.55.9">Is 55:7-9</reference>; Mal 3:6). I do not, like man, change when once I have made a covenant of everlasting love, as with Israel (<reference osisRef="Num.23.19">Nu 23:19</reference>). We measure God by the human standard, and hence are slow to credit fully His promises; these, however, belong to the faithful remnant, not to the obstinately impenitent.<div eID="gen22701" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22702" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in the midst of thee--</hi>as peculiarly thy God (<reference osisRef="Exod.19.5">Ex 19:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Exod.19.6">6</reference>).<div eID="gen22702" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22703" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">not enter into the city--</hi>as an enemy: as I entered Admah, Zeboim, and Sodom, utterly destroying them, whereas I will not utterly destroy thee. Somewhat similarly Jerome: "I am not one such as human dwellers in a city, who take cruel vengeance; I save those whom I correct." Thus "not man," and "in the midst of thee," are parallel to "into the city." Though I am in the midst of thee, it is not as man entering a rebellious city to destroy utterly. Maurer needlessly translates, "I will not come in wrath." <div eID="gen22703" type="x-p"/>
entries.72e5324668ec68745a68b6e4817ddc1148b08f6d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12393"/><div sID="gen22704" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12393"/><hi type="bold">10. he shall roar like a lion--</hi>by awful judgments on their foes (<reference osisRef="Isa.31.4">Is 31:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.25.26-Jer.25.30">Jr 25:26-30</reference>; <reference osisRef="Joel.3.16">Joe 3:16</reference>), calling His dispersed "children" from the various lands of their dispersion.<div eID="gen22704" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22705" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">shall tremble--</hi>shall flock in eager agitation of haste.<div eID="gen22705" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22706" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">from the west--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Zech.8.7">Zec 8:7</reference>). Literally, "the sea." Probably the Mediterranean, including its "isles of the sea," and maritime coast. Thus as <reference osisRef="Hos.11.11">Ho 11:11</reference> specifies regions of Africa and Asia, so here Europe. <reference osisRef="Isa.11.11-Isa.11.16">Is 11:11-16</reference>, is parallel, referring to the very same regions. On "children," see <reference osisRef="Hos.1.10">Ho 1:10</reference>. <div eID="gen22706" type="x-p"/>
entries.23d8ca60c210792be0144253283708aa33d101b5: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12394"/><div sID="gen22707" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12394"/><hi type="bold">11. tremble--</hi>flutter in haste.<div eID="gen22707" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22708" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">dove--</hi>no longer "a silly dove" (<reference osisRef="Hos.7.11">Ho 7:11</reference>), but as "doves flying to their windows" (<reference osisRef="Isa.60.8">Is 60:8</reference>).<div eID="gen22708" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22709" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in their houses--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Ezek.28.26">Eze 28:26</reference>). Literally, "upon," for the Orientals live almost as much upon their flat-roofed houses as in them. <div eID="gen22709" type="x-p"/>
entries.f9e790417ed53927ded58fc2c2d1e387a209c41a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12395"/><div sID="gen22710" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12395"/>12. Maurer joins this verse with the twelfth chapter. But as this verse praises Judah, whereas <reference osisRef="Hos.12.2">Ho 12:2</reference> censures him, it must belong rather to the eleventh chapter and a new prophecy begins at the twelfth chapter. To avoid this, Maurer translates this verse as a censure, "Judah wanders with God," that is, though having the true God, he wanders after false gods.<div eID="gen22710" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22711" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">ruleth with God--</hi>to serve God is to reign. Ephraim wished to rule without God (compare <reference osisRef="1Cor.4.8">1Co 4:8</reference>); nay, even, in order to rule, cast off God's worship [Rivetus]. In Judah was the legitimate succession of kings and priests.<div eID="gen22711" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22712" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">with the saints--</hi>the holy priests and Levites [Rivetus]. With the fathers and prophets who handed down the pure worship of God. Israel's apostasy is the more culpable, as he had before him the good example of Judah, which he set at naught. The parallelism ("with God") favors Margin, "With THE Most Holy One." <chapter eID="Hos.11"/>

entries.debfde2e33a418082a1732bc4cd2a8a99f73e1e1: <div eID="gen33864" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen33865" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen33866" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen33866" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen33865" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen33867" type="x-p"/> This chapter gives a very pathetic representation of God's tender and affectionate regard for Israel, by metaphors chiefly borrowed from the conduct of mothers toward their tender offspring. From this, occasion is taken to reflect on their ungrateful return to the Divine goodness, and to denounce against them the judgments of the Almighty, <reference osisRef="Hos.11.1-Hos.11.7">Hos 11:1-7</reference>. But suddenly and unexpectedly the prospect changes. Beams of mercy break frown the clouds just now fraught with vengeance. God, to speak in the language of men, feels the relentings of a tender parent; his bowels yearn; his mercy triumphs; his rebellious child shall yet be pardoned. As the lion of the tribe of Judah, he will employ his power to save his people, he will call his children from the land of their captivity; and, as doves, they will fly to him, a faithful and a holy people, <reference osisRef="Hos.11.8-Hos.11.12">Hos 11:8-12</reference>. <div eID="gen33867" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33868" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen33868" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33869" type="x-p"/> When Israel was a child - In the infancy of his political existence. <div eID="gen33869" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33870" type="x-p"/> I loved him, and called my son out of Egypt - Where he was greatly oppressed; and in this I gave the proof of my love. I preserved my people in their affliction there, and brought them safely out of it.
entries.1f99f1624dd4428c647542e92576659015f57031: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen33870" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33871" type="x-p"/> I taught Ephraim also to go - An allusion to a mother or nurse teaching a child to walk, directing it how to lift and lay its feet, and supporting it in the meantime by the arms, that it may use its feet with the greater ease. This is a passage truly pathetic.
entries.3967ecec11780a65d7334761130f2133bb40a64b: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen33871" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33872" type="x-p"/> I drew them with cords of a man - This is a reference to leading strings, one end of which is held by the child, the other by the nurse, by which the little one, feeling some support, and gaining confidence, endeavors to walk. God, their heavenly Father, made use of every means and method to teach them to walk in the right and only safe path; for, as the Targum says, "As beloved children are drawn I drew them by the strength of love." <div eID="gen33872" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33873" type="x-p"/> That take of the yoke on their jaws - I did every thing that mercy could suggest, and justice permit, to make their duty their delight and profit. There appears to be here an illusion to the moving and pulling forward the collar or yoke of beasts which have been hard at work, to let in the cool air between it and their neck, so as to refresh them, and prevent that heat, which with the sweat would scald their necks, and take off not only the hair, but the skin. I have often done this at the land ends, in ploughing, when at the turnings the cattle were permitted a few moments to draw their breath after the hard pull that terminated the furrow at either end of the field: - <div eID="gen33873" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33874" type="x-p"/> And I laid meat unto them - Giving them at the same time a bite of grass or hay, to encourage them to go on afresh. The metaphor is strong and expressive; and he who ever had or saw the management of cattle in the plough or cart must admire it. Thus God acted with the people on whose necks was the yoke of his law. How many privileges, advantages, and comforts did he mingle with his precepts, to make them at once a righteous and happy people!
entries.fbf97450a04c590e22f6338a076093a6f3d7430a: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen33874" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33875" type="x-p"/> He shall not return into - Egypt - I have brought them thence already, with the design that the nation should never return thither again; but as they have sinned, and forfeited my favor and protection, they shall go to Assyria; and this because they refused to return to me. This view of the verse removes every difficulty.
entries.a2653a23d08879258ffda27d840980df6091c655: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen33875" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33876" type="x-p"/> The sword shall abide on his cities - Israel was agitated with external and intestine wars from the time of Jeroboam the Second. Although Zechariah his son reigned twelve years, yet it was in continual troubles; and he was at last slain by the rebel Shallum, who, having reigned one month, was slain by Menahem. Pekahiah succeeded his father Menahem, and reigned two years, and was killed by Pekah, son of Remaliah. He joined Rezin, king of Syria, and made an irruption into the land of Judah; but Ahaz having obtained succor from Tiglath-Pileser, king of Assyria, Pekah was defeated, and the tribes of Reuben, Gad, Naphtali, and the half-tribe of Manasseh, were carried away captives by the Assyrian king; and in a short time after, Hosea, son of Elah, slew Pekah and usurped the kingdom, which he could not possess without the assistance of Shalmaneser, who for his services imposed a tribute on the Israelitish king. Wishing to rid himself of this yoke, he applied to the king of Egypt; but this being known to Shalmaneser, he came against Samaria, and after a three years' siege took and destroyed it. Thus the sword rested on their cities; it continued in the land till all was ruined. See Calmet.
entries.225e0c32b9d9c4a261d9328613811f88587c27a2: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen33876" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33877" type="x-p"/> Though they called them to the Most High - Newcome is better: "And though they call on him together because of the yoke, he will not raise it. He shall receive no refreshment." See the metaphor, <reference osisRef="Hos.11.4">Hos 11:4</reference> (note).
entries.74d9d8d22b32d95d479b61c1ebbe9e2b45ab74f1: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen33877" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33878" type="x-p"/> How shall I give thee up - See the notes on <reference osisRef="Hos.6.4">Hos 6:4</reference>, where we have similar words from similar feeling. <div eID="gen33878" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33879" type="x-p"/> Mine heart is turned within me - Justice demands thy punishment; Mercy pleads for thy life. As thou changest, Justice resolves to destroy, or Mercy to save. My heart is oppressed, and I am weary with repenting - with so frequently changing my purpose. All this, though spoken after the manner of men, shows how merciful, compassionate, and loath to punish the God of heaven is. What sinner or saint upon earth has not been a subject of these gracious operations?
entries.59980d6ec7cb3ddafa85110de6e166e4d3593fee: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen33879" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33880" type="x-p"/> I will not execute - Here is the issue of this conflict in the Divine mind. Mercy triumphs over Judgment; Ephraim shall be spared. He is God, and not man. He cannot be affected by human caprices. They are now penitent, and implore mercy; he will not, as man would do, punish them for former offenses, when they have fallen into his hand. The holy place is in Ephraim, and God is in this holy place; and he will not go into the cities, as he did into Sodom and Gomorrah, to destroy them. Judgment is his strange work. How exceedingly affecting are these two verses!
entries.602e9d8a464dbf52c154faf671b89caa16010ada: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen33880" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33881" type="x-p"/> They shall walk after the Lord - They shall discern the operations of his providence, when, <div eID="gen33881" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33882" type="x-p"/> He shall roar like a lion - When he shall utter his majestic voice, Cyrus shall make his decree. The people shall tremble - be in a state of commotion; every one hurrying to avail himself of the opportunity to return to his own land.
entries.aa9d3651fdd14a0d96779a2ed4539ea233d69f66: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen33882" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33883" type="x-p"/> They shall tremble as a bird - Those of them that are in Egypt shall also be called thence, and shall speed hither as a bird. Those in Assyria shall also be called to return, and they shall flee as doves to their windows. All shall, in the fullness of time, return to their own land. And, <div eID="gen33883" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33884" type="x-p"/> I will place them in their houses, saith the Lord - They shall have their temple once more, and all their holy ordinances.
entries.c1990b50d4968f6063c2e5ccd016d0098d0337ca: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen33884" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33885" type="x-p"/> Ephraim compasseth me about with lies - I think this verse does not well unite with the above; it belongs to another subject, and should begin the following chapter, as in the Hebrew. <div eID="gen33885" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33886" type="x-p"/> Judah yet ruleth with God - There is an allusion here to <reference osisRef="Gen.32.24">Gen 32:24</reference>, where Jacob having "wrestled with the Angel," had his name changed to Israel, one that rules with God. That glory the Israelites had lost by their idolatry; but Judah still retained the true worship, and alone deserved the name of Israel. <div eID="gen33886" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33887" type="x-p"/> Bp. Newcome translates this clause thus: - "But hereafter they shall come down a people of God, even a faithful people of saints." <div eID="gen33887" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen33888" type="x-p"/> Even allowing this to be the most correct view of the original, I do not see what we gain by this change.  <chapter eID="Hos.11"/> <div eID="gen33888" type="x-p"/>

entries.dc42aa35b782df3e3788bd955c63e75ad31780b4: Hos 11:1-2 <div eID="gen16254" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16255" type="x-p"/> The prophet goes back a third time (cf. Hos 10:1; Hos 9:10) to the early times of Israel, and shows how the people had repaid the Lord, for all the proofs of His love, with nothing but ingratitude and unfaithfulness; so that it would have merited utter destruction from off the earth, if God should not restrain His wrath for the sake of His unchangeable faithfulness, in order that, after severely chastening, He might gather together once more those that were rescued from among the heathen. Hos 11:1. <hi type="italic">“When Israel was young, then I loved him, and I called my son out of Egypt.</hi> Hos 11:2. <hi type="italic">Men called to them; so they went away from their countenance: they offer sacrifice to the Baals, and burn incense to the idols.” </hi> Hos 11:1 rests upon <reference osisRef="Exod.4.22-Exod.4.23">Exo 4:22-23</reference>, where the Lord directs Moses to say to Pharaoh, “Israel is my first-born son; let my son go, that he may serve me.” Israel was the son of Jehovah, by virtue of its election to be Jehovah’s peculiar people (see at <reference osisRef="Exod.4.22">Exo 4:22</reference>). In this election lay the ground for the love which God showed to Israel, by bringing it out of Egypt, to give it the land of Canaan, promised to the fathers for its inheritance. The adoption of Israel as the son of Jehovah, which began with its deliverance out of the bondage of Egypt, and was completed in the conclusion of the covenant at Sinai, forms the first stage in the carrying out of the divine work of salvation, which was completed in the incarnation of the Son of God for the redemption of mankind from death and ruin. The development and guidance of Israel as the people of God all pointed to Christ; not, however, in any such sense as that the nation of Israel was to bring forth the son of God from within itself, but in this sense, that the relation which the Lord of heaven and earth established and sustained with that nation, was a preparation for the union of God with humanity, and paved the way for the incarnation of His Son, by the fact that Israel was trained to be a vessel of divine grace. All essential factors in the history of Israel point to this as their end, and thereby become types and material prophecies of the life of Him in whom the reconciliation of man to God was to be realized, and the union of God with the human race to be developed into a personal unity. It is in this sense that the second half of our verse is quoted in <reference osisRef="Matt.2.15">Mat 2:15</reference> as a prophecy of Christ, not because the words of the prophet refer directly and immediately to Christ, but because the sojourn in Egypt, and return out of that land, had the same significance in relation to the development of the life of Jesus Christ, as it had to the nation of Israel. Just as Israel grew into a nation in Egypt, where it was out of the reach of Canaanitish ways, so was the child Jesus hidden in Egypt from the hostility of Herod. But Hos 11:2 is attached thus as an antithesis: this love of its God was repaid by Israel with base apostasy. קראוּ, they, viz., the prophets (cf. Hos 11:7; 2Ki 17:13; <reference osisRef="Jer.7.25">Jer 7:25</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.25.4">Jer 25:4</reference>; Zec 1:4), called to them, called the Israelites to the Lord and to obedience to Him; but they (the Israelites) went away from their countenance, would not hearken to the prophets, or come to the Lord (<reference osisRef="Jer.2.31">Jer 2:31</reference>). The thought is strengthened by כּן, with the כּאשׁר of the protasis omitted (Ewald, §360, <hi type="italic">a</hi>): as the prophets called, so the Israelites drew back from them, and served idols. בּעלים as in Hos 2:15, and פּסלים as in 2Ki 17:41 and <reference osisRef="Deut.7.5">Deu 7:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Deut.7.25">Deu 7:25</reference> (see at <reference osisRef="Exod.20.4">Exo 20:4</reference>).
entries.a037f2598f93e8c295c9e6b438f54b30b88f00dd: Hos 11:3-4 <div eID="gen16255" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16256" type="x-p"/> Nevertheless the Lord continued to show love to them. Hos 11:3, Hos 11:4. <hi type="italic">“And I, I have taught Ephraim to walk: He took them in His arms, and they did not know that I healed them. I drew them with bands of a man, with cords of love, and became to them like a lifter up of the yoke upon their jaws, and gently towards him did I give (him) food.” </hi>תּרגּלתּי, a <hi type="italic">hiphil</hi>, formed after the Aramaean fashion (cf. Ges. §55, 5), by hardening the ה into ת, and construed with ל, as the <hi type="italic">hiphil</hi> frequently is (e.g., Hos 10:1; <reference osisRef="Amos.8.9">Amo 8:9</reference>), a <hi type="italic">denom</hi>. of רגל, to teach to walk, to guide in leading-strings, like a child that is being trained to walk. It is a figurative representation of paternal care foz a child’s prosperity. קחם, <hi type="italic">per aphaeresin</hi>, for לקחם, like קח for לקח in Eze 17:5. The sudden change from the first person to the third seems very strange to our ears; but it is not uncommon in Hebrew, and is to be accounted for here from the fact, that the prophet could very easily pass from speaking in the name of God to speaking of God Himself. קח cannot be either an infinitive or a participle, on account of the following word זרועתיו, <hi type="italic">his</hi> arms. The two clauses refer chiefly to the care and help afforded by the Lord to His people in the Arabian desert; and the prophet had <reference osisRef="Deut.1.31">Deu 1:31</reference> floating before his mind: “in the wilderness the Lord thy God bare thee, as a man doth bear his son.” The last clause also refers to this, רפאתים pointing back to <reference osisRef="Exod.15.26">Exo 15:26</reference>, where the Lord showed Himself as the physician of Israel, by making the bitter water at Marah drinkable, and at the same time as their helper out of every trouble. In Hos 11:4, again, there is a still further reference to the manifestation of the love of God to Israel on the journey through the wilderness. חבלי אדם, cords with which men are led, more especially children that are weak upon their feet, in contrast with ropes, with which men control wild, unmanageable beasts (<reference osisRef="Ps.32.9">Psa 32:9</reference>), are a figurative representation of the paternal, human guidance of Israel, as explained in the next figure, “cords of love.” This figure leads on to the kindred figure of the yoke laid upon beasts, to harness them for work. As merciful masters lift up the yoke upon the cheeks of their oxen, i.e., push it so far back that the animals can eat their food in comfort, so has the Lord made the yoke of the law, which has been laid upon His people, both soft and light. As הרים על על does not mean to take the yoke away from (מעל) the cheeks, but to lift it above the cheeks, i.e., to make it easier, by pushing it back, we cannot refer the words to the liberation of Israel from the bondage of Egypt, but can only think of what the Lord did, to make it easy for the people to observe the commandments imposed upon them, when they were received into His covenant (<reference osisRef="Exod.24.3">Exo 24:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Exod.24.7">Exo 24:7</reference>), including not only the many manifestations of mercy which might and ought to have allured them to reciprocate His love, and yield a willing obedience to His commandments, but also the means of grace provided in their worship, partly in the institution of sacrifice, by which a way of approach was opened to divine grace to obtain forgiveness of sin, and partly in the institution of feasts, at which they could rejoice in the gracious gifts of their God. ואט is not the first pers. imperf. <hi type="italic">hiphil</hi> of נטה (“I inclined myself to him;” Symm., Syr., and others), in which case we should expect ואט, but an adverb, softly, comfortably; and אליו belongs to it, after the analogy of 2Sa 18:5. אוכיל is an anomalous formation for אאכיל, like אוביד for אאביד in <reference osisRef="Jer.46.8">Jer 46:8</reference> (cf. Ewald, §192, <hi type="italic">d</hi>; Ges. §68, 2, Anm. 1). Jerome has given the meaning quite correctly: “and I gave them manna for food in the desert, which they enjoyed.”
entries.0dc15525ac29c760a3b8a7fa2b2abbfa2c1a93b8: Hos 11:5-7 <div eID="gen16256" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16257" type="x-p"/> By despising this love, Israel brings severe punishment upon itself. Hos 11:5. <hi type="italic">“It will not return into the land of Egypt; but Asshur, he is its king, because they refused to return.</hi> Hos 11:6. <hi type="italic">And the sword will sweep round in its cities, and destroy its bolts, and devour, because of their counsels.</hi> Hos 11:7. <hi type="italic">My people is bent upon apostasy from me: and if men call it upwards, it does not raise itself at all.” </hi> The apparent contradiction between the words, “It will not return into the land of Egypt,” and the threat contained in Hos 8:13; Hos 9:3, that Israel should return to Egypt, ought not to lead us to resort to alterations of the text, or to take לא in the sense of לו, and connect it with the previous verse, as is done by the lxx, Mang., and others, or to make an arbitrary paraphrase of the words, either by taking לא in the sense of הלא, and rendering it as a question, “Should it not return?” equivalent to “it will certainly return” (Maurer, Ewald, etc.); or by understanding the return to Egypt as signifying the longing of the people for help from Egypt (Rosenmüller). The emphatic הוּא of the second clause is at variance with all these explanations, since they not only fail to explain it, but it points unmistakeably to an antithesis: “Israel will not return to Egypt; but Asshur, it shall be its king,” i.e., it shall come under the dominion of Assyria. The supposed contradiction is removed as soon as we observe that in Hos 8:13; Hos 9:3, Hos 9:6, Egypt is a type of the land of bondage; whereas here the typical interpretation is precluded partly by the contrast to Asshur, and still more by the correspondence in which the words stand to <hi type="italic">Hos 11:1</hi>. Into the land from which Jehovah called His people, Israel shall not return, lest it should appear as though the object, for which it had been brought out of Egypt and conducted miraculously through the desert, had been frustrated by the impenitence of the people. But it is to be brought into another bondage. ואשּׁוּר is appended adversatively. Asshur shall rule over it as king, because they refuse to return, sc. to Jehovah. The Assyrians will wage war against the land, and conquer it. The sword (used as a principal weapon, to denote the destructive power of war) will circulate in the cities of Israel, make the round of the cities as it were, and destroy its bolts, i.e., the bolts of the gates of the fortifications of Ephraim. <hi type="italic">Baddı̄m</hi>, poles (Exo 25:13.), cross-poles or cross-beams, with which the gates were fastened, hence bolts in the literal sense, as in <reference osisRef="Job.17.16">Job 17:16</reference>, and not tropically for “princes” (Ges.), <hi type="italic">electi</hi> (Jer., Chald., etc.). “On account of their counsels:” this is more fully defined in Hos 11:7. נעמּי, <hi type="italic">and</hi> my people (= <hi type="italic">since</hi> my people) are harnessed to apostasy from me (<hi type="italic">meshūbhâthı̄</hi>, with an objective suffix). תּלוּאים, lit., suspended on apostasy, i.e., not “swaying about in consequence of apostasy or in constant danger of falling away” (Chald., Syr., Hengst.), since this would express too little in the present context and would not suit the second half of the verse, but impaled or fastened upon apostasy as upon a stake, so that it cannot get loose. Hence the constructing of תּלה with ל instead of על or ב (<reference osisRef="2Sam.18.10">2Sa 18:10</reference>), may be accounted for from the use of the verb in a figurative sense. על־על, <hi type="italic">upwards</hi> (על as in Hos 7:16), do they (the prophets: see Hos 11:2) call them; but <hi type="italic">it</hi> does not rise, sc. to return to God, or seek help from on high. רומם <hi type="italic">pilel</hi>, with the meaning of the <hi type="italic">kal</hi> intensified, to make a rising, i.e., to rise up. This explanation appears simpler than supplying an object, say “the soul” (<reference osisRef="Ps.25.1">Psa 25:1</reference>), or “the eyes” (<reference osisRef="Ezek.33.25">Eze 33:25</reference>).
entries.12578597dc8a2791b9fe82686387610cb9a84b10: Hos 11:8-9 <div eID="gen16257" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16258" type="x-p"/> They deserved to be utterly destroyed for this, and would have been if the compassion of God had not prevented it. With this turn a transition is made in Hos 11:8 from threatening to promise. Hos 11:8. <hi type="italic">“How could I give thee up, O Ephraim! surrender thee, O Israel! how could I give thee up like Admah, make thee like Zeboim! My heart has changed within me, my compassion is excited all at once.</hi> Hos 11:9. <hi type="italic">I will not execute the burning heat of my wrath, I will not destroy Ephraim again: for I am God, and not man, the Holy One in the midst of thee: and come not into burning wrath.” </hi>“How thoroughly could I give thee up!” sc. if I were to punish thy rebellion as it deserved. <hi type="italic">Nâthan</hi>, to surrender to the power of the enemy, like <hi type="italic">miggēn</hi> in Gen 14:20. And not that alone, but I could utterly destroy thee, like Admah and Zeboim, the two cities of the valley of Siddim, which were destroyed by fire from heaven along with Sodom and Gomorrha. Compare <reference osisRef="Deut.29.22">Deu 29:22</reference>, where Admah and Zeboim are expressly mentioned along with the cities of Sodom and Gomorrha, which stand alone in Gen 19:24. With evident reference to this passage, in which Moses threatens idolatrous Israel with the same punishment, Hosea simply mentions the last two as quite sufficient for his purpose, whereas Sodom and Gomorrha are generally mentioned in other passages (<reference osisRef="Jer.49.18">Jer 49:18</reference>; cf. <reference osisRef="Matt.10.15">Mat 10:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.10.12">Luk 10:12</reference>). The promise that God will show compassion is appended here, without any adversative particle. My heart has turned, changed in me (על, lit., upon or with me, as in the similar phrases in <reference osisRef="1Sam.25.36">1Sa 25:36</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.8.18">Jer 8:18</reference>). יחד נכמרוּ, in a body have my feelings of compassion gathered themselves together, i.e., my whole compassion is excited. Compare <reference osisRef="Gen.43.30">Gen 43:30</reference> and 1Ki 3:26, where, instead of the abstract <hi type="italic">nichūmı̄m</hi>, we find the more definite <hi type="italic">rachămı̄m</hi>, the bowels as the seat of the emotions. עשׂה חרון אף, to carry out wrath, to execute it as judgment (as in <reference osisRef="1Sam.28.18">1Sa 28:18</reference>). In the expression לא אשׁוּב לשׁחת, I will not return to destroy, שׁוּב may be explained from the previous נהפּך לבּי. After the heart of God has changed, it will not return to wrath, to destroy Ephraim; for Jehovah is God, who does not alter His purposes like a man (cf. <reference osisRef="1Sam.15.29">1Sa 15:29</reference>; Num 23:19; Mal 3:6), and He shows Himself in Israel as the Holy One, i.e., the absolutely pure and perfect one, in whom there is no alternation of light and darkness, and therefore no variableness in His decrees (see at <reference osisRef="Exod.19.6">Exo 19:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.6.3">Isa 6:3</reference>). The difficult expression בּעיר cannot mean “into a city,” although it is so rendered by the ancient versions, the Rabbins, and many Christian expositors; for we cannot attach any meaning to the words “I do not come into a city” at all in harmony with the context. עיר signifies here <hi type="italic">aestus irae</hi>, the heat of wrath, from עוּר, <hi type="italic">effervescere</hi>, just as in <reference osisRef="Jer.15.8">Jer 15:8</reference> it signifies the heat of alarm and anxiety, <hi type="italic">aestus animi</hi>.
entries.98787e3b8ac254a3f63a5d496e2bb0d84c137b49: Hos 11:10-11 <hi type="italic">“They will go after Jehovah; like a lion will He roar; for He will roar: and sons will tremble from the sea.</hi> Hos 11:11. <hi type="italic">Tremble like birds out of Egypt, and like doves out of the land of Asshur: and I cause them to dwell in their houses, is the saying of Jehovah.” </hi> When the Lord turns His pity towards the people once more, they will follow Him, and hasten, with trembling at His voice, from the lands of their banishment, and be reinstated by Him in their inheritance.
